results.taskOutput:
Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 with:
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - container: rec-engine with containerPort: 80
  - Security configuration matches the stable deployment (no explicit securityContext)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine to send traffic to both stable and canary by broadening the selector:
  - selector: app: recommendation-engine (removed version filter)
  - kept type: ClusterIP
  - kept port: 80 and targetPort: 8080 (same as before to match runtime port expectations)

Result
- With 2 replicas on engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas on engine-v2-1, the Service will distribute roughly 50/50 across the 4 endpoints.

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get pods -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns describe svc recommendation-engine
- Send a few test requests and check which pod serves them (e.g., expose pod name in response or curl Exec into pods and check access logs).

Rollback/adjust
- To stop canary: set Service selector back to include version: v2.0, or scale engine-v2-1 to 0.
- To change traffic split: adjust replica counts proportionally (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary for ~75/25).

Steps.message:
namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 with:
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - container: rec-engine with containerPort: 80
  - Security configuration matches the stable deployment (no explicit securityContext)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine to send traffic to both stable and canary by broadening the selector:
  - selector: app: recommendation-engine (removed version filter)
  - kept type: ClusterIP
  - kept port: 80 and targetPort: 8080 (same as before to match runtime port expectations)

Result
- With 2 replicas on engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas on engine-v2-1, the Service will distribute roughly 50/50 across the 4 endpoints.

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get pods -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns describe svc recommendation-engine
- Send a few test requests and check which pod serves them (e.g., expose pod name in response or curl Exec into pods and check access logs).

Rollback/adjust
- To stop canary: set Service selector back to include version: v2.0, or scale engine-v2-1 to 0.
- To change traffic split: adjust replica counts proportionally (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary for ~75/25).

Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 with:
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - container: rec-engine with containerPort: 80
  - Security configuration matches the stable deployment (no explicit securityContext)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine to send traffic to both stable and canary by broadening the selector:
  - selector: app: recommendation-engine (removed version filter)
  - kept type: ClusterIP
  - kept port: 80 and targetPort: 8080 (same as before to match runtime port expectations)

Result
- With 2 replicas on engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas on engine-v2-1, the Service will distribute roughly 50/50 across the 4 endpoints.

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get pods -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns describe svc recommendation-engine
- Send a few test requests and check which pod serves them (e.g., expose pod name in response or curl Exec into pods and check access logs).

Rollback/adjust
- To stop canary: set Service selector back to include version: v2.0, or scale engine-v2-1 to 0.
- To change traffic split: adjust replica counts proportionally (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary for ~75/25).

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the container command to run: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which caused the container to exit immediately and the pod to CrashLoop.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment without the custom command/args so nginx runs with its default startup.
- Set the container port to 8080 (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: app-7f7b5548bd-zf2qn in crashloop-test is 1/1 Running, Restarts: 0.

Notes
- If there’s a Service pointing to this Deployment, ensure its targetPort is 8080 to match the unprivileged nginx image. I can adjust or create a Service if needed.
- If you intended to run a specific startup command, tell me what it should be and I’ll update the Deployment accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
I found the root cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Events showed: ProvisioningFailed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC (it had no data yet).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with an existing StorageClass: standard.

Current status
- The pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns is now Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane.
- The nginx container is up and the volume is attached.

How to verify
- kubectl get pod -n homepage-ns homepage-pod
- kubectl get pvc -n homepage-ns homepage-pvc
- kubectl describe pvc -n homepage-ns homepage-pvc

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or a different size/access mode, tell me and I’ll adjust the PVC accordingly.

outputSteps.content:
I found the root cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Events showed: ProvisioningFailed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC (it had no data yet).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with an existing StorageClass: standard.

Current status
- The pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns is now Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane.
- The nginx container is up and the volume is attached.

How to verify
- kubectl get pod -n homepage-ns homepage-pod
- kubectl get pvc -n homepage-ns homepage-pvc
- kubectl describe pvc -n homepage-ns homepage-pvc

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or a different size/access mode, tell me and I’ll adjust the PVC accordingly.

I found the pod was failing its health checks because the container was listening on port 8080 while the probes and Service targeted port 80 with non-existent paths.

What I fixed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Liveness/readiness probes now hit / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (the nginx-unprivileged image listens there).
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Running and healthy (readiness/liveness passing).
- Service endpoints point to port 8080.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster:
  - curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
  - or curl http://10.96.255.35 (your Service ClusterIP)

If you want external access, I can create an Ingress with a host/path of your choice.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role only allowed listing apps/Deployments, not core/Pods. So the pod-reader ServiceAccount had no permission to list pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to allow pods in the core API group:
  - verbs: get, list, watch on resources: pods
  - Kept the existing permission to list apps/Deployments

Your current RBAC
- ServiceAccount: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader
- Role: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role (now includes pods permissions)
- RoleBinding: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding binding the SA to the Role

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
  Expected: yes
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  Note: It may return “No resources found” if there are no pods in that namespace.

If you need this SA to read pods in other namespaces or cluster-wide, we can switch to a ClusterRole + (Cluster)RoleBinding.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role only allowed listing apps/Deployments, not core/Pods. So the pod-reader ServiceAccount had no permission to list pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to allow pods in the core API group:
  - verbs: get, list, watch on resources: pods
  - Kept the existing permission to list apps/Deployments

Your current RBAC
- ServiceAccount: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader
- Role: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role (now includes pods permissions)
- RoleBinding: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding binding the SA to the Role

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
  Expected: yes
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  Note: It may return “No resources found” if there are no pods in that namespace.

If you need this SA to read pods in other namespaces or cluster-wide, we can switch to a ClusterRole + (Cluster)RoleBinding.

  - Kept the existing permission to list apps/Deployments

- Role: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role (now includes pods permissions)
- RoleBinding: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding binding the SA to the Role

- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  Note: It may return “No resources found” if there are no pods in that namespace.

If you need this SA to read pods in other namespaces or cluster-wide, we can switch to a ClusterRole + (Cluster)RoleBinding.

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found and fixed.

Root cause
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pod label: app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints.
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80, so even with endpoints traffic would hit the wrong container port.

What I changed
- Updated the Service in namespace web to:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (name: http)

Current state (verified)
- Endpoints for Service web/nginx now show 1 healthy endpoint:
  - 10.244.0.37:8080 (pod nginx-987f59664-6cssw)
- The Deployment pod is Running and Ready.

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- From any pod in the cluster, curl/wget the Service:
  - http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - or http://nginx (from same namespace)

Note on external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster.
- If you need external access, say which you prefer and I can set it up:
  - NodePort (simple; exposes on each node’s IP and a high port)
  - LoadBalancer (cloud environments)
  - Ingress (via an Ingress controller; needs host/path and class)

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. The scheduler couldn’t place the pods (FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector), so the Service had no endpoints and callers saw “connection refused.”

What I changed to fix it
- Updated the Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment to remove the nodeSelector so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current state
- Pods are now running:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-8hh25 – Running (10.244.0.39)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-r4g5t – Running (10.244.0.40)
- Service endpoints are populated:
  - web-app-service → 10.244.0.39:80, 10.244.0.40:80
- This should clear the connection refused errors.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- Or port-forward a pod: kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward deploy/web-app-deployment 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080

If you intended to target special nodes
- Option A: Label the desired node(s) and then reintroduce the selector:
  - kubectl label nodes <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Re-add nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu to the Deployment.
- Option B: Use node affinity/tolerations if you need more flexible placement rules.

Recommendations
- Add readinessProbe/livenessProbe on port 80 to prevent routing before the app is ready.
- Pin the image to a specific tag instead of latest (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29).
- Set resource requests/limits for predictable scheduling.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. The scheduler couldn’t place the pods (FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector), so the Service had no endpoints and callers saw “connection refused.”

What I changed to fix it
- Updated the Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment to remove the nodeSelector so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current state
- Pods are now running:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-8hh25 – Running (10.244.0.39)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-r4g5t – Running (10.244.0.40)
- Service endpoints are populated:
  - web-app-service → 10.244.0.39:80, 10.244.0.40:80
- This should clear the connection refused errors.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- Or port-forward a pod: kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward deploy/web-app-deployment 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080

If you intended to target special nodes
- Option A: Label the desired node(s) and then reintroduce the selector:
  - kubectl label nodes <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Re-add nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu to the Deployment.
- Option B: Use node affinity/tolerations if you need more flexible placement rules.

Recommendations
- Add readinessProbe/livenessProbe on port 80 to prevent routing before the app is ready.
- Pin the image to a specific tag instead of latest (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29).
- Set resource requests/limits for predictable scheduling.

      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

  labels:
    app: web-app

  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:

        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. The scheduler couldn’t place the pods (FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector), so the Service had no endpoints and callers saw “connection refused.”

What I changed to fix it
- Updated the Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment to remove the nodeSelector so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current state
- Pods are now running:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-8hh25 – Running (10.244.0.39)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-r4g5t – Running (10.244.0.40)
- Service endpoints are populated:
  - web-app-service → 10.244.0.39:80, 10.244.0.40:80
- This should clear the connection refused errors.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local
- Or port-forward a pod: kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward deploy/web-app-deployment 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080

If you intended to target special nodes
- Option A: Label the desired node(s) and then reintroduce the selector:
  - kubectl label nodes <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Re-add nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu to the Deployment.
- Option B: Use node affinity/tolerations if you need more flexible placement rules.

Recommendations
- Add readinessProbe/livenessProbe on port 80 to prevent routing before the app is ready.
- Pin the image to a specific tag instead of latest (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29).
- Set resource requests/limits for predictable scheduling.

Done. I created the pod communication-pod in the multi-container-logging namespace as requested.

What’s set up:
- Two containers in spec.containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, serving on port 8080
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox, running: sh -c "tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log"
- Shared volume: logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Readiness: web-server has an HTTP readinessProbe on path /, port 8080 (pod becomes Ready when Nginx serves traffic)

Current state:
- Pod status is Running and Ready.

Optional verification:
- Check pod: kubectl -n multi-container-logging get pod communication-pod
- Port-forward and hit Nginx: kubectl -n multi-container-logging port-forward pod/communication-pod 8080:8080, then curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/
- See access logs: kubectl -n multi-container-logging exec -it communication-pod -c logger -- sh -c 'tail -n +1 /var/log/nginx/access.log | head -n 50'

Steps.message:
Done. I created the pod communication-pod in the multi-container-logging namespace as requested.

What’s set up:
- Two containers in spec.containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, serving on port 8080
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox, running: sh -c "tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log"
- Shared volume: logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Readiness: web-server has an HTTP readinessProbe on path /, port 8080 (pod becomes Ready when Nginx serves traffic)

Current state:
- Pod status is Running and Ready.

Optional verification:
- Check pod: kubectl -n multi-container-logging get pod communication-pod
- Port-forward and hit Nginx: kubectl -n multi-container-logging port-forward pod/communication-pod 8080:8080, then curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/
- See access logs: kubectl -n multi-container-logging exec -it communication-pod -c logger -- sh -c 'tail -n +1 /var/log/nginx/access.log | head -n 50'

results.taskOutput:
Done.

What I set up
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (clusterIP: None) for stable network IDs
- StatefulSet: db
  - replicas: 3 (with ordered, stable identities db-0, db-1, db-2)
  - volumeClaimTemplates: data (1Gi, ReadWriteOnce) mounted at /data
  - initContainer writes /data/test with the string initial_data if it doesn’t already exist
  - main container: busybox sleeping (so pods stay up)

Then I scaled the StatefulSet back down to 1 replica.

Notes
- The StatefulSet uses a volumeClaimTemplate, so PVCs are named:
  - data-db-0, data-db-1, data-db-2
- PVC retention is set to Retain when scaled or deleted, so the PVCs (and the test file) persist even after scaling down.

How to verify (optional)
- Check pods: kubectl -n statefulset-test get pods -l app=db
- Check PVCs: kubectl -n statefulset-test get pvc
- Verify file on a pod (example for db-0): kubectl -n statefulset-test exec -it db-0 -- sh -c "cat /data/test"  # should output: initial_data

Current state
- Desired replicas: 1. The controller will converge to one running pod (db-0) and the other replicas will terminate; their PVCs remain.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Immediate failure on start:
  - PipelineRun tekton-eval/failed-run has condition:
    - reason: CouldntGetTask
    - message: Pipeline tekton-eval/broken-pipeline can’t be Run; it contains Tasks that don’t exist: Couldn’t retrieve Task "missing-task": tasks.tekton.dev "missing-task" not found
  - Associated TaskRun failed-run-missing-pipeline shows:
    - reason: TaskRunResolutionFailed
    - podName: "" (no pod ever started)
    - message: tasks.tekton.dev "missing-task" not found
- Pipeline spec:
  - Pipeline tekton-eval/broken-pipeline has a single taskRef:
    - name: missing-task (kind: Task)
- Task presence:
  - No Task named missing-task exists in namespace tekton-eval.
  - Attempt to list ClusterTask returned “no matches for kind ClusterTask” (ClusterTask CRD not present on this cluster).
- Events confirm the same root cause (Failed/InternalError with “missing-task not found”).
- Pipeline-as-Code and Operator context:
  - No pipelinesascode.tekton.dev Repository CRD found (both v1alpha1 and v1beta1): Pipelines-as-Code is not installed or not in use here.
  - No operator.tekton.dev TektonConfig CRD found: Tekton Operator is not installed; Tekton Pipelines likely installed standalone.

Likely root cause
The Pipeline references a Task that does not exist in the namespace (and there is no ClusterTask CRD available). This is either:
- A missing installation of the intended Task, or
- A name mismatch in the pipeline’s taskRef, or
- A leftover reference to a former ClusterTask after migrating to a Tekton Pipelines version without ClusterTask support.

Recommended next action
- Choose one of the following remediations:
  1) Install the Task in tekton-eval with the exact name missing-task.
     - If this was meant to come from Tekton Hub or another repo, apply that Task manifest into tekton-eval.
  2) Correct the pipeline to reference the right Task name (if it was mistyped).
  3) If you previously relied on ClusterTask:
     - Migrate to a namespaced Task and reference it via taskRef.name, or
     - Use a resolver (e.g., git/hub/bundles) and define taskRef.resolver with the required params. Note that ClusterTask CRD is not present on this cluster.

- Verify:
  - kubectl get task missing-task -n tekton-eval (should exist)
  - kubectl get pipeline broken-pipeline -n tekton-eval (taskRef should point to an existing Task or use a resolver)

- Re-run:
  - After fixing, create a new PipelineRun or restart this one with the same spec.
  - If you’d like, I can restart it for you once the Task is in place.
